full_text:
I’m in my third decade of producing this article, and while the content herein has evolved, my goal remains simple: I want to give you an edge in winning your league by providing a sensible roadmap for your season-long drafts.

As usual, the plan focuses on two things: 1) finding the optimal route for roster construction based on positional scarcity and 2) finding the right or best players to draft.

I’ve watched the ADP develop, observed the trends, and studied the players and their situations in depth, as usual. I’ve also pored over data, kept up with all the news, and reached out to my contacts for insider information and insights, like [the July 20 Fantasy Points podcast with](https://www.fantasypoints.com/media/podcasts/episode/adam-schefter-s-2026-fantasy-football-news-and-notes#/) [*ESPN*](https://www.fantasypoints.com/media/podcasts/episode/adam-schefter-s-2026-fantasy-football-news-and-notes#/)[’s Adam Schefter,](https://www.fantasypoints.com/media/podcasts/episode/adam-schefter-s-2026-fantasy-football-news-and-notes#/) in which I basically asked him all NFL Insider questions presented as fantasy questions.

I’ve also drafted a lot this summer, mostly over at the [FFPC](https://myffpc.com/cms/public/), so I’ve been testing my plan against the toughest opponents: high-stakes players.

No draft plan is entirely static, so there’s always some flexibility in play, but my plan this year has never been more definitive. And striving for more accuracy, I’ve never been more selective about which players I back as targets.

Here’s a look at what’s contained in this manifesto:

1.  A quick look at my approach and what I’m thinking this year.
2.  “The 12,” which are my top 12 essential player targets for optimal roster construction.
3.  My plan of attack at each position, along with the specific players I’m targeting and when.
4.  “The Dirty 30,” which are 30 players I’m passing on this year at ADP.
5.  The “Hansen 50” list (my 50 targets within the top 200).
6.  My favorite picks this year by round (1-18).
7.  The Draft Plan in action.

{{CTA|FFPC|omit=\[none\]}}

### My Approach/What I’m thinking

I’ll get into the nuances of each position below, but just a few notes before we begin:

+   As usual, I’m looking to rank the players better than they are in the marketplace in terms of their ADPs and industry rankings. Most of the players listed in my plan are market-beaters because I think they are mispriced.

+   For most of my targets, it’s about the player *plus* the cost. I focus on upside for later picks, but the further a player is down the ADP board, the lower the expectations should be.
+   I’m focused on ascending players while passing on those in decline, since most players have their “career year” at 28 or younger. However, I’ve been more willing to back older players the last couple of years, and I once again have a collection of aged players who I believe are being undervalued this year (likely due to their age).
+   Due to this year’s weak draft class along with a few poor landing spots, I’m not into most of the consensus top 10 rookies this year.
+   I’m always looking for buying opportunities with good players, so I’ll also look at assets that were depressed the year before due to injury, poor situations, etc.

And by the way, many of the opinions expressed here have been discussed throughout the year [on my podcast](https://www.fantasypoints.com/media/podcasts/show/the-fantasy-points-podcast#/) with __Brian Drake__, available on the site or wherever you get your pods, so be sure to subscribe! We’re doing two podcasts a week in August with the Monday pods discussing each week of preseason action.

### __“The Twelve”__

There are usually only 7-15 players who actually matter in each season, especially in this day and age, when replacement-level players are more plentiful than ever. I’ve always focused on finding legit needle-movers, which is why I’m usually chasing breakout and career seasons, and why I’ve focused on young, ascending players my whole career.

My primary goal with this list is to identify 12 players with impactful upside to help you win a championship, but these players are also critical to implementing my plan of attack this season because of when they can be acquired and how they fit within the roster from a roster-building standpoint.

{{PAYWALL}}

My list wasn’t incredible last year, since I was in on Vikings __J.J. McCarthy__ and __TJ Hockenson__, along with __Calvin Ridley__, which was horrible.

But there were league-winners on last year’s list, like __Jaxon Smith-Njigba__, __Jonathan Taylor__, and __Davante Adams__, along with solid picks at their ADPs like __Chase Brown__, __Jameson Williams__, __TreVeyon Henderson__, and __Deebo Samuel__. I also included __Ricky Pearsall__ on the list, and he was great (but only when healthy, which was rare).

My goal this year is to have fewer misses, plain and simple, so while I’d love to include him because he fits the bill perfectly, I'm banning Ricky P from the list until he shows he can get through a season relatively unscathed.

1.  __CHRISTIAN WATSON__ (WR, GB, Round 6) — I generally see WR as less of a priority this year because the position isn’t as top-heavy as it’s been the last few seasons, and since the quality depth down the board is better than ever, so I see no need to load up on WR in the first 4-5 rounds with Watson available in Round 6. I legitimately think he will produce like a 2nd or 3rd-round pick, if healthy, so he’s an excellent pick as a WR3 in Round 6.

+   __TYLER WARREN__ (TE, Ind, Round 5) — He’s got a massive opportunity this year with top target __Michael Pittman__ gone, so I can see a world where Warren finishes as the overall TE1 on the season. You should be able to secure a pair of high-end options at RB and WR in the first four rounds before all the truly appealing options are off the board. And by the 5th round, Warren should stand out as one of the best players available and one of the highest-impact starters on the board.
+   __BROCK BOWERS__ (TE, LV, Round 2) — Coming off an injury-plagued campaign that has dropped him down the board 10-12 picks, and with discernable upgrades at QB and offensive coordinator/playcaller, Bowers looks like a great buy in Round 2. Based on the 2026 ADP, one can acquire an elite RB like __Jonathan Taylor__ in Round 1, get Bowers in Round 2, and then an anchor-type WR like __Chris Olave__ in Round 3, which looks like a great foundational start.
+   __SAQUON BARKLEY__ (RB, Phi, Round 2) — I’m attempting to get Barkley right three years in a row, since I was high on him in 2024, and very convinced he was going to drop off in 2025. He’s still in a top-10 environment, and he’s been healthy now four years in a row. I do expect some speed bumps in a new offense, so he won’t touch his ‘24 production. But if healthy, Barkley should have a strong season somewhere in between his 2024 and 2025 levels.
+   __TERRY MCLAURIN__ (WR, Was, Round 5) — McLaurin has a huge opportunity on the receiver-poor Commanders, so he has a chance to produce at a WR1 level, as he did in 2024 (WR7 overall). That makes him a viable WR2, and a *great* WR2 in Round 5 if you go heavy on RBs and also take a stud TE like __Brock Bowers__.
+   __CAM SKATTEBO__ (RB, NYG, Round 4) — The vibes are not good for the Giants, given the __Malik Nabers__ situation, so I think they’re going to lean heavily on Skattebo if his health allows it. He’s a good fit for __Greg Roman__’s running scheme, the OL should be solid enough, and this offense will be all about power football, so a healthy Skattebo should produce. He’s a big key because he’s one of the last RBs off the board whom I’d feel good about as my RB2. I’d take him in the fourth, but he’s an even better selection if he slips to the early 5th.
+   __MICHAEL PITTMAN__ (WR, Pit, Round 9) — Pittman’s ADP is sure to rise, but he’ll probably still end up on *all* my teams because I think he’s one of the most mispriced players on the board this year in Round 9. I truly see him as producing at a top-25 level, and even if things don’t go as well as I’m expecting, he’ll still be a solid pick.
+   __CHUBA HUBBARD__ (RB, Car, Round 7) — Hubbard isn’t considered a trendy pick this year because of the presence of a healthy __Jonathon Brooks__, who tore his right ACL at the end of 2023 and again in 2024. But Hubbard is still the favorite to be the lead back and has an edge in experience and in pass protection. Even if Brooks is healthy all year, Hubbard should have a healthy role, and he should deliver a solid ROI as a seventh-round pick — but he’s also a sneaky league-winner if Brooks proves ineffective or if he succumbs to another serious injury.
+   __TREVOR LAWRENCE__ (QB, Jax, Round 8) — Considering the player’s floor and ceiling, along with cost, I’m completely convinced that Lawrence and __Justin Herbert__ are the best two QB picks on the board this year. Both have easy top-5 potential, so it’s just a question of which player I like better. I’m 100% convinced that the Jags offense will pick up where it left off, and since Lawrence is going a few picks after Herbert, I’ve been leaning lately on Lawrence as my favorite.
+   __JUSTIN HERBERT__ (QB, LAC, Round 8) — It’s a coin flip for me between Lawrence and Herbert with a very, very slight lean to Lawrence heading into the preseason. I do think Herbert might be safer, but Lawrence may have more upside, since LA will certainly be run-heavy.
+   __BREECE HALL__ (RB, NYJ, Round 3) — I’ve been high on Breece in the past, but I bailed on backing Hall last summer due to the horrible vibes with the Jets, which was more of a good call than not. But Hall’s situation this year has improved, so his outlook is as well. All we need is a competent offense and for Hall to enjoy relatively good health, and Hall should be a solid asset. If he can avoid injury, he should easily clear 300+ touches, despite more talk of a committee backfield.
+   __SAM LAPORTA__ (TE, Det) — While I’m in love with __Tyler Warren__ as a fifth-round pick this summer, LaPorta could easily be the better value going off the board around 30 picks later in Round 8.

### __The Overall 2026 Plan__

I will get things rolling by outlining my plan of action at each position. I don’t anticipate my plan changing significantly as the summer progresses, but I will make some tweaks, including additions and subtractions, to my target lists up until Week 1.

__Please Note__: I’m still sticking to my usual process of tweaking my rankings projections, and [I regularly publish them on my own rankings page](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/rankings/redraft/qb?season=2024#/).

I’m also using those positional rankings to regularly rank the top 200 players for PPR, non-PPR, and 0.5 PPR formats. I do these overall rankings manually so I can rank the players in the sweet spot between where they are going off the board and where they should be. You can find these as PDFs in the Downloads section of the site, located under [Downloads > Cheat Sheets](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/downloads#/cheat-sheets).

\> *All ADPs are as of* *__July 21, 2026__**.* *__Unless otherwise noted, I’m always referring to 1-QB, non-TE-Premium PPR leagues__**. Most of the analysis can apply to leagues with between 10 and 12 teams. Players are listed by order of their ADP, and I rank my favorite 50 picks below based on player and cost.*

### The Quarterback Plan

To cut right to the chase, 2026 may be the deepest QB class in history, so I’m not paying up for one this year, just like last year, when roughly 60% of the top-12 producers (FPG) were drafted after the 8th round. The only early-round QB I might be willing to draft at his ADP is __Drake Maye__, who is very young and may still be ascending.

Buffalo’s __Josh Allen__ continues to be Superman, but he’s in a run-heavy offense, and he’s no longer young, having been battered now for eight NFL seasons.

Although Vegas has them with the second-highest projected win total this year, which is a good sign, veteran __Lamar Jackson__ looked like a shell of his former self last year, and I worry about his body breaking down. He has excelled in his first year in a new offense before, but it’s yet another system with a young and thinned/weaker receiving corps.

While a baller and a previous favorite, __Joe Burrow__, has proven to be unreliable, having missed six or more games in half of his six seasons. He’s been going off the board around the exact same time as non-QBs like __Terry McLaurin__ and __Tyler Warren__, two players I love this year. I’d take both over Burrow knowing I can still draft a (potentially) elite QB later.

In 2024, __Jayden Daniels__ barely stayed in one piece for a brilliant rookie season, but his ability to stay on the field in 2026 is a legit question, and he’s working with a weak receiving corps while breaking in a new OC who’s never called plays.

These guys not only have issues, but they’re also expensive. One or more of them could easily hit this year and deliver the goods, but I’m not paying a premium for any of them.

I’m OK with __Jalen Hurts__, __Caleb Williams__, __Dak Prescott__, and __Patrick Mahomes__ at their ADPs, but I’m not actively targeting them. These guys should be mostly fine, but Hurts has more downside these days with the Tush Push’s waning effectiveness and is breaking in a new system; Caleb is still inaccurate; Prescott is older and doesn’t run anymore; Mahomes is coming off his ACL.

This year, as covered in my [Guru’s Guys article](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/gurus-guys-best-fantasy-football-picks), I have six QBs I’m targeting, and they are:

__TREVOR LAWRENCE__ (Jax, 92) — Should have a great floor and also has a nice ceiling.

__JUSTIN HERBERT__ (LAC, 84) — Feel great about the offense, but they will be run-heavy.

The margin between these two is very, very close, so I plan on using the preseason news and vibes to break the tie by mid-August.

__BROCK PURDY__ (SF, 103) — Mr. TD is uber-productive when healthy, but his lack of health is one reason he’s a value.

__KYLER MURRAY__ (Min, 151) — I firmly believe Kyler will succeed for fantasy in Minnesota, and that he will be used a lot as a runner near the goal.

__TYLER SHOUGH__ (NO, 144) — I see an outside chance that he’s pretty special for fantasy in this solid environment.

__MALIK WILLIS__ (Mia, 146) — Willis can finish with fewer than 200 passing yards a game and still produce because of his legs.

\> For deeper analysis on these players, check out the [Guru’s Guys article](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/gurus-guys-best-fantasy-football-picks).

### The Running Back Plan

I never wavered from my inclination to acquire at least one “anchor” RB early in this draft plan, so “Zero RB” was never a thing for me. And with NFL teams daring opponents to run the ball, you can be damn sure I’m into drafting running backs early this year. That’s especially because they’re flying off the board at pre-2020 levels these days, pushing the WR talent down the board a tad.

First and foremost, based on the flow of the player talent in the first 2-3 rounds, and their massive appeal, if I have a top-2 pick this year, I’m taking either __Jahmyr Gibbs__ or __Bijan Robinson__. If I do, I should get access to some good players like __Brock Bowers__, __Chris Olave__, __Derrick Henry__, and __A.J. Brown__ for my next two picks in the top-25 overall.

If I’m drafting in the 3-5 range, I’m probably looking at WR, since I see __Puka Nacua__, __Ja'Marr Chase__, and __Amon-Ra St. Brown__ in a tier by themselves and the only super-elite options this year.

At pick six overall or later, if I can get __Jonathan Taylor__, one of my favorite players of all time and a big part of my draft plan every year, I’m doing it.

At picks 7-8, I’m likely going back to WR for __Jaxon Smith-Njigba__ or __CeeDee Lamb__.

In the latter stages of Round 1, I’m not opposed to __James Cook__, __De'Von Achane__, or __Ashton Jeanty__, and I’ll probably take one of them either at the end of Round 1 or early in Round 2. That’s because there’s a chance that I won’t get access to a viable RB1 when I’m 30-36 picks into a draft in Round 3.

One player I am opposed to is __Christian McCaffrey__, who I was vehemently against in 2024 and still out on in 2025. I’m 1-for-2 on CMC the last two years, and I like my chances to go 2-for-3 given he’s another year older and looked like a fullback running the ball last year. I get it; he’ll get a million targets, but I just can’t take a player with his profile that high.

I’m not going to account for every possible scenario here, but to summarize my plan of attack: I'll be set with two RBs after four rounds. Outside of my affinity for Gibbs, Bijan, and JT, my 2nd- to 4th-round targets, as analyzed more in-depth in my [Guru’s Guys article](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/gurus-guys-best-fantasy-football-picks), and listed in order of ADP, are:

__OMARION HAMPTON__ (LAC, 14) — Fits the bill in terms of youth and versatility, and offense is on the rise.

__SAQUON BARKLEY__ (Phi, 16) — Price is down one round from 2025, and I’m expecting a bounce-back.

__CHASE BROWN__ (Cin, 18) — Relatively safe with a huge role and receiving production, and upside if he gets the TDs.

__BREECE HALL__ (NYJ, 31) — Team outlook is improved, and he’s still an elite talent with a huge role.

__JAVONTE WILLIAMS__ (Dal, 33) — Extremely safe and steady as bellcow in explosive offense.

__CAM SKATTEBO__ (NYG, 45) — If healthy, the offense should go through him. He’s important because once he’s off the board, we see a tier drop, and I don’t love the next few options off the board as an RB2.

Ideally, I’m able to draft two of the RBs promoted above among Gibbs, Bijan, JT, Barkley, Hampton, Brown, Javonte, and Skattebo. But it’s tough to say I’ll be able to get two of those eight in the majority of my drafts, so my next two player targets could suffice as my RB2, especially since I should be strong at WR/TE if I wait until Round 5 to draft my RB2.

__DAVID MONTGOMERY__ (Hou, 53) — He’s the clear primary back for the AFC South favorites with an elite defense, and he can produce on all three downs and score short rushing TDs.

__D'ANDRE SWIFT__ (Chi, 57) — I gave him some love here last year, and he logged a stellar campaign, and with no changes of note this year, I’m expecting a repeat of 2025.

__CHUBA HUBBARD__ (Car, 78) — Mr. Every-Other-Year is due, and while they don’t have an elite QB, it’s a good environment overall. Chuba also has a big upside if __Jonathan Brooks__ is not a meaningful contributor for whatever reason.

__JADARIAN PRICE__ (Sea, 81) — He’s raw, but he’s also an explosive play waiting to happen. They will need him, so he’s a good calculated risk at his affordable price.

__RICO DOWDLE__ (Pit, 84) — Rico has proven a lot, and I expect him to be the clear lead runner for his old coach __Mike McCarthy__, who will try to run the rock to hide his old QB.

__RACHAAD WHITE__ (Was, 108) — Well in the mix for a meaningful role with the pass-catching duty on all but lock-down when he signed his contract, White could easily settle in as a 200+ touch guy in this weak backfield.

__CHRIS RODRIGUEZ__ (Jax, 146) — This is something of a bet against __Bayshul Tuten__, but I think all three Jaguar backs will have roles and C-Rod played for __Liam Coen__ in college and could steal goal line carries.

__ALVIN KAMARA__ (NO, 150) — Hey, a player with Kamara’s pedigree in the 13th round? I’ll take it, especially since they re-did Kamara’s contract and since I don’t think __Travis Etienne__ is good.

\> Again, for deeper analysis on these players, check out the [Guru’s Guys article](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/gurus-guys-best-fantasy-football-picks).

### The Wide Receiver Plan

Last year, I felt there were only 5-6 truly elite WRs, and this year I think there are even fewer of them, so I’m probably going to be drafting a wideout in Round 1 about 50% of the time.

As stated above, if I have a crack at either __Jahmyr Gibbs__ or __Bijan Robinson__ at the top of the draft, I’m taking one of them.

But if I don’t have access to Gibbs or Bijan, then I’m taking __Puka Nacua__, __Ja'Marr Chase__, or __Amon-Ra St. Brown__, in that order.

If those two RBs and three WRs are gone, and __Jonathan Taylor__ is available, I’m taking JT.

But otherwise, if I’m picking in the 8-12 range, there’s a better than 50% chance that I’ll be acquiring either __Jaxon Smith-Njigba__, __CeeDee Lamb__, or __Justin Jefferson__. I view those three as very solid WR anchors and first-round picks.

But here’s the main point regarding the wideouts this year: I’ve never seen more quality depth within the top-100 overall players, and there are more quality “sleepers” than ever 100+ picks into a draft. I definitely think it’s important to get at least 1-2 high-end options, especially since secondary receivers on NFL teams fell flat last year. But there are some good pockets for drafting WRs this year, even in Rounds 6-9, so I don’t see the need to load up with 3-4 WRs in the first 4-5 rounds.

Excluding the six wideouts above who are likely first-round picks, here are my WR targets:

__NICO COLLINS__ (Hou, 22) — He’s a little boring, but Collins looks appealing in Round 2 for teams that pick at the top of Round 1 and open with an RB.

__CHRIS OLAVE__ (NO, 28) — If I opt to open with non-WRs in the first two rounds, Olave looks like an excellent target in Round 3.

__DEVONTA SMITH__ (Phi, 38) — The durable and reliable Smith is getting an upgraded coaching staff and role in 2026 under respected new OC __Sean Mannion__.

__ZAY FLOWERS__ (Bal, 39) — His data is great, the new offense is drawing rave reviews, and barring an extension this year, he’ll be gunning for a JSN-like payday all year long.

__TERRY MCLAURIN__ (Was, 50) — Opportunity is knocking for McLaurin, who has looked healthy and re-energized by the new offense and is due for a bounce-back.

__D.J. MOORE__ (Buf, 56) — He’s fairly priced, so I’m buying his upgraded role and supporting cast under new Bills HC __Joe Brady__, who Moore excelled under in Carolina.

__ROME ODUNZE__ (Chi, 61) — If he’s healthy, with a year in the system and fewer mouths to feed, I see Odunze as a good bet to ascend this season with top-24 potential.

__CHRISTIAN WATSON__ (GB, 63) — Based on his incredible 2025 showing and the thinned-out Packers receiving corps, a WR1 season may be inevitable if he can avoid injury (a colossal *if*).

__ALEC PIERCE__ (Ind, 67) — As long as he doesn’t miss a lot of camp coming off his injury, his game should continue to expand with more volume, and Indy is paying him a ton of money so he’ll get the ball plenty.

__PARKER WASHINGTON__ (Jax, 87) — Washington’s 2025 season was too impressive to ignore, and that includes his work on the outside. I like the Jag passing game to continue to roll, and Washington feels both safe and interesting for upside.

__RICKY PEARSALL__ (SF, 94) — His numbers are borderline elite when healthy in this excellent environment, so if he can somehow find a way to avoid injury, he’ll be a great pick.

__MICHAEL PITTMAN__ (Pit, 99) — One of the most mispriced players this year, I love Pittman to be their volume receiver, and I believe __Aaron Rodgers__ can still get him the ball consistently in the short/intermediate area.

__JOSH DOWNS__ (Ind, 115) — He’ll likely take some reps outside, which is a big development, since he ran only 18.5% of his routes from the outside last season. If he can stay in one piece with an increase in snaps and routes, then he should produce.

__XAVIER WORTHY__ (KC, 122) — Worthy has never made my list before, but I’m interested in buying this season. That’s based on their need at receiver, the OC change, and his depressed cost.

__JALEN COKER__ (Jax, 136) — Similar to Washington but to a lesser extent, Coker was too good to ignore last year, and he’ll likely also get more outside snaps this season. His QB will likely cap his upside, but I like Coker for WR depth.

__JALEN MCMILLAN__ (TB, 160) — Flashed as a rookie with 8 TDs on only 58 targets and has clicked well with __Baker Mayfield__, so I would not be shocked if McMillan winds up being their second-leading receiver.

__JERRY JEUDY__ (Cle, 161) — The Browns drafted two promising wideouts this past spring, but Jeudy is the incumbent No. 1 receiver, and the veteran is still only 27 years old. As only a 14th-round pick, he should deliver a surprising ROI for those who dig deep.

__JALEN NAILOR__ (LV, 167) — Veteran __Tre Tucker__ looks like a value in his own right, but the new staff did hand-pick Nailor in free agency this year, and he played with __Kirk Cousins__ in Minnesota running a similar offense, so I think he has more upside than the markets recognize.

__DEEBO SAMUEL__ (FA, 171) — I’ve been a big Deebo guy from Day 1, and I even had him as one of my top-12 targets last year, and he crushed his ADP with a WR25 finish overall on the season. Wherever he lands, it’ll likely be in an offense that both needs him and is able to utilize him.

__CALVIN RIDLEY__ (Ten, 200) — I liked him as a 7th-rounder last year, and it went horribly, but the offense should improve considerably with a new OC and some experience for his QB, and Ridley is now properly cast as a #2, so he might log one more solid season.

### The Tight End Plan

By far the worst part of my Draft Plan last year was my endorsement of __TJ Hockenson__, which was too much of a projection, and it was based on very little, since Hockenson’s QB had zero NFL starts under his belt.

I won’t make a mistake like that again, especially since TE has otherwise been one of my most accurate positions to handicap.

I’m not high on __Trey McBride__ this year, but I am perfectly willing to draft an elite TE in 2026, so my first player target is a 2nd-rounder because he’s also one of the most dangerous players to ever play the position.

__BROCK BOWERS__ (LV, 20) — Gets a massive upgrade with new HC __Klint Kubiak__, who has called Bowers a “football robot from heaven.” Bowers will also get an upgrade at QB, and he’ll be getting a huge contract extension at season’s end if he has a big year

I’m certainly going to draft Bowers over my next TE, but this guy is also likely available 3-4 rounds later, so he’s my favorite TE pick on the board.

I’m willing to take a shot with __Colston Loveland__, as well, but he’s probably going to go off the board 10-12 picks after this guy:

__TYLER WARREN__ (Ind, 55) — I think it’s fair to expect Warren’s usage to increase in year two, so a little TD love, along with minimal time missed, should result in an elite season if __Daniel Jones__ is able to play the majority of their games.

If I miss out or pass on Warren, I’m not totally against __Harold Fannin__ or __Kyle Pitts__, but I’m not very into their QBs, so they’re not making my list.

If I’m in Round 6 with at least a pair of RBs and WRs I feel good about, and I’m not into the RBs/WRs on the board, then I’m certainly willing to pivot right over to this TE:

__TUCKER KRAFT__ (GB, 70) — His QB trusts him majorly, and his volume is increasing this year for sure. Among 54 TEs with at least 25 targets, Kraft was second with .62 FP/RR, and he was third at the position with a stellar 2.54 YPRR, so his potential is blatantly obvious.

If it just so happens that Bowers, Warren, and Kraft aren’t in the cards for me, I’ll be queuing up this veteran, who’s well in the mix for my pick for TE value of the year.

__SAM LAPORTA__ (Det, 91) — In 18 career games with a route share of 75% or higher, LaPorta has averaged a whopping 15.9 FPG, so considering his high-end ability and a limited target tree in Detroit, with more routes run this year, he could be the best TE value on the board this year.

The TE position is very deep this year, so if I somehow miss out on Bowers, Warren, Kraft, and LaPorta, then I’m probably going to roll with an old guy listed below, at least as my TE2. My next group of targets contains those two old guys and two younger guys.

__JAKE FERGUSON__ (DAL, 105) — He’s still young and in a top offense, and if __George Pickens__ has any problems playing under the franchise tag, then the team’s reliance on Ferguson will increase.

__TRAVIS KELCE__ (KC, 107) — Excluding Weeks 16-18 without __Pat Mahomes__, Kelce posted 12.8 FPG, which was good for TE5 in FPG. Kelce is fired up about the return of OC __Eric Bieniemy__, so I see another strong season at 37 years old a la __Tony Gonzalez__’ final season (83/859/8).

__TE__: Sam Laporta

__Flex__: Rome Odunze/Rico Dowdle

### __TL;DR__

So there you have it! I’m not a big TL;DR guy, and I know they’re usually placed at the top of the article, but here’s my TL;DR for this year’s draft plan:

+   The RBs are back en vogue, so you should plan on getting two of them in the first 4-5 rounds to ensure you’re at least solid at the position.

+   This is the deepest class of QBs I’ve ever seen, and I can make cases *against* four of the top-5 QBs going off the board, so I REALLY want to wait on QB and take my starter no earlier than the seventh round.
+   I see fewer elite WR options this year, so I value the true studs, and I want at least one of the consensus top-12 players. However, the depth is incredible, so if I have only 1-2 WRs through Round 5, I’m fine with it.
+   It’s also a good year to pay up for an elite TE, and there are only five of them (if we’re lucky).

Considering I’ve tightened up my criteria for my picks, I don’t think I’ll have to change much, barring any major developments, but I’ll certainly be adding and removing some players and tweaking the entire article throughout the summer, with the final update coming Labor Day weekend.

Happy Drafting!

As a former national champion college debate coach, I learned that the best way to make tough calls is simple: debate the best evidence on both sides.

The average fantasy manager is sharper than ever, but groupthink makes it difficult to determine the best side of many close arguments. There is more good data than ever, but also *much* more misleading evidence as optimism peaks in July.

This article will debate the bull and bear cases and answer three of fantasy’s hardest questions:

+ De’Von Achane: Top 5 RB or Regression Candidate?

+ Carolina’s RB1: Chuba Hubbard or Jonathon Brooks?
+ Chicago’s Top Threat: Luther Burden, Colston Loveland, or Rome Odunze?

\> For those of you who want to jump right to the bottom line, simply Ctrl+F “decision” to skip ahead!

### __De’Von Achane:__ Top 5 RB or Regression Candidate?

De’Von Achane was once a Round 1 fixture following his RB5 finish in 2025, but he has since fallen to a DraftKings ADP of 18.8. [*Fantasy Points*](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/projections/season/rb#/)[’](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/projections/season/rb#/) [projections](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/projections/season/rb#/) have Achane finishing RB5 with 19.2 FP/G, but many are out on him in 2026. Will Achane produce another Top 5 RB season or drown in the abyss of one of the NFL’s worst offenses?

##### The bear case

A broken Miami offense, a wave of stacked boxes, and a decline in explosives and receiving will be too much to overcome.

Waddle’s departure leaves behind what *ESPN* Writer Bill Barnwell calls one of the [worst WR rooms in recent NFL history](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/49154825/ranking-nfl-teams-offensive-groups-wr-rb-te-2026-season-best-playmakers), and defenses will stack the box to dare unproven first-year starter Malik Willis to beat them through the air.

Willis mustered only 3 total passing TDs across three starts in Green Bay and now pilots an offense whose most proven pass catcher is Greg Dulcich. *Fantasy Points* Senior Writer Tom Brolley cites Achane as [Miami’s only legit offensive weapon](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/nfl-player-props-rushing-yards-leader#/), leaving defenses with little guesswork.

Achane excelled due to an unsustainable explosives rate. His 2025 mark of 10.1% of runs going for 15+ yards was the most of any 120+ carry RB season in *Fantasy Points Data* history. A whopping 46.1% of his rushing yards came on these runs, the most of any RB in 2025. With more stacked boxes and no other threats to stop, explosives will be harder to come by.

Achane’s receiving output will also take a hit. He goes from the QB who targets RBs at the highest rate in Tua Tagovailoa to the QB who targets them at the [lowest rate](https://x.com/FantasyPts/status/2073029283778376147?s=20) in Willis, and [RB targets](https://x.com/SmolaDS/status/2074472869887705260?s=20) dip with run-first QBs. Achane has historically struggled mightily [without Tua](https://x.com/SideHustleFF/status/2077821284138811760?s=20).

He also goes from a Mike McDaniel offense to one piloted by new OC Bobby Slowik. Slowik [does not target his RBs](https://x.com/EthanKreagerFF/status/2062887118024605705?s=20) at a high rate or [creatively shift them out of the backfield](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2026671462686294114?s%3D20&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1784476888474898&usg=AOvVaw1QEv8SYw6Gy4PwxTZNj4yD), where Achane has averaged 3.0 or more FP/G every season of his career. Slowik’s Texans were 22nd and 18th in yards before contact, while McDaniel’s Dolphins were 12th, 1st, 14th, and 4th. Miami may choose the 219-pound Willis at the goal line over the 191-pound Achane. Tua had no designed carries inside the ten over the past two seasons, but Willis received 18.2% of his team’s designed looks inside the ten*.* That creates another obstacle to touchdown equity on a Dolphins offense with a bottom-four Vegas implied points per game (19.1).

Achane is a spectacular talent. Bet on him to be Top 5 again one day, but not this year. 2026 is a [transition season](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/48933195/miami-dolphins-rebuild-trades-offseason-otas-jeff-hafley-roster-nfl-draft) for new GM Jon-Eric Sullivan and HC Jeff Hafley. Achane has a bright long-term outlook but is very unlikely to be Top 5 in 2026.

##### The bull case

Achane is an unstoppable one-man offense whom no stacked box can fully contain.

Achane is Miami’s best player by a mile and was the new regime’s [first big extension](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/48763689/dolphins-rb-devon-achane-reach-4-year-extension). Miami will stink, most likely, but Achane is no stranger to losing. Achane does [some of his best work](https://x.com/KyleM_FF/status/2069178806905242074?s=20) in losing game scripts, with *Fantasy Points* contributor Kyle Menton noting he finished second among all RBs with 18.9 FP/G in losses the past two seasons.

His production has always overcome Miami’s woes. Brolley notes Achane [did more with less](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/nfl-player-props-rushing-yards-leader#/) in 2025, leading the league in YPC (5.67) in a bottom-12 offense (by EPA/P) behind a [bottom-five offensive line](https://x.com/RyanPaganetti/status/2076410843093201230?s=20). *Fantasy Points* CEO Scott Barrett notes that Achane [leads all RBs in YPC](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/2075217407895814572?s=20) by a country mile over the past three seasons, with a 5.62 YPC mark that edges out Bo Jackson’s 5.40 YPC for the best career YPC since the mid-1950s.

Achane is an equally dangerous pass catcher, with Barrett noting that Achane leads all RBs in receptions over the last two seasons (145) and a 4.4 receptions-per-game mark that rivals those of Terry McLaurin and D.J. Moore. Slowik’s Texans rarely targeted RBs, but he went to Achane early and often as Miami’s senior passing game coordinator last year. Achane still finished as RB5 under Slowik despite Miami finishing dead last in plays per game.

The 2025 Miami offense powering Achane’s Top 5 finish was a sinkhole. Waddle mustered only 56.9 receiving YPG in 2025, and Tua struggled to hit 190.0 passing YPG. *Fantasy Points Data* COO Brett Whitefield notes the [McDaniel magic left Miami](https://www.youtube.com/live/XNglAudHMOI?si=DVExdr36oleyTiLh&t=2241) long before the coach departed. Ecosystem matters, but talent and workload also play a big role, and it is hard to name an RB with more talent who will play a more central role in their offense in 2026.

Stacked boxes were made to be beaten by Achane, who had the [second-best YPC](https://x.com/NFL_Researcher/status/2034654377223619017?s=20) mark against stacked boxes in 2025 and the [most carries of 10+ yards](https://x.com/TheFFRealist/status/2022307042094964922?s=20) against those looks of any RB. Willis doesn’t have Tua’s passing chops, but Achane is the perfect RPO complement to Willis. Willis is a more dangerous red zone rusher than Tua, but Achane’s output never depended on red zone rushing. Achane finished RB5 despite only three red zone rushing touchdowns in 2025, fewer than Bam Knight. Run-first QBs do target RBs less, but they also [increase rushing efficiency and YPC](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/season/2021/konami-code-revisited-mobile-qb-revolution#/).

Good receiving backs can produce great outputs in bad offensive setups with scrambling QBs. Alvin Kamara led all RBs in 2021 with an 18.2% team target share while averaging 18.1 FP/G per *Fantasy Points Data* playing on a Saints team that cycled through Taysom Hill and backup QBs. Leonard Fournette produced career-best receiving marks in 2019 with 76 catches and 522 receiving yards on a ground-bound 6-10 Jaguars team with Gardner Minshew.

Achane’s profile carries both extreme risk and reward, but his ADP only prices in the risk. He is currently going behind Chase Brown and Kenneth Walker, but Achane is the only RB in that group to produce 20 FP/G over a season. Very few RBs match Achane's ceiling, and his skillset and usage give him a steady floor.

##### The judge’s decision

__De’Von Achane will finish Top 5.__ __Even a depressed TD output on a team struggling for 5 wins won’t be enough to hold back “the__ [__Tyreek Hill of RBs__](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/1651610655097597954?s=20)__.”__

The *Fantasy Points* projections bake in each worst-case scenario. Achane is projected for a career-low 2.8 receiving TDs, a second-worst mark of 7.4 rushing TDs, and declines in his rushing and receiving yards vs. 2025, yet still projects in the Top 5. His 71.3 projected receptions are a reasonable target in an offense with few other weapons. Although that 71.3 mark is 7 receptions off from his career high, it’s still a ceiling few other RBs can hit.

It’s easy to argue the 2026 Dolphins will be awful, defenses will stack the box, and many key offensive cogs departed. It’s hard to dispute any of that. But it’s harder still to argue that Achane has struggled against stacked boxes, or that any of Tua, Waddle, or McDaniel were at their peak with Miami in 2025.

2026 will likely see the worst version of the Miami offense in recent memory, but it will also feature the biggest dose of Achane. If he creeps back into a Round 1 ADP, it’s worth taking the bear case against Achane seriously, but at his current ADP of 18.8, I’m a strong buy on the bull case. Achane is the modern NFL’s version of [Birdman](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9iCd6UHR-3I): he stays fly in any weather.

### __Carolina’s RB1:__ Hubbard or Brooks?

This could be one of the most consequential debates of 2026. The RB1 role in a Dave Canales offense is a gold mine for expected fantasy points.

 We can use XFP per team play (from @FantasyPtsData ) to measure overall RB fantasy opportunity. Leaders since 2021: 1. Christian McCaffrey - 0.31 2. Klint Kubiak's RB1 - 0.30 3. Alvin Kamara - 0.29 4. Joe Mixon - 0.28 5. Josh Jacobs - 0.27 6. Dave Canales' RB1 - 0.27 — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) July 7, 2025 

The drumbeat for Jonathon Brooks is growing. He’s up almost [100 spots in ADP](https://x.com/KyleM_FF/status/2062533518505419106?s=20) since January and has [lapped Chuba Hubbard](https://x.com/TheOGfantasy/status/2069891112160919787?s=20) in many high-stakes formats. Many have dubbed him the [potential Carolina RB1](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2064012198888808911?s=20). Will Hubbard hold off another rising threat, or will Brooks take the Panthers RB1 crown by the end of the season?

##### The case for Brooks

The more explosive RB with [better pass-catching chops](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2061995479206903823?s=20) will return to good health and seize the RB1 role by season’s end.

It’s not hard to see why the first RB off the board in 2024, who is [only 2.5 months older than Jadarian Price](https://x.com/jmthrivept/status/2063706082669941159?s=20), is drawing more looks than the 27-year-old Hubbard.

Unlike Hubbard, Brooks is a [promising receiving threat](https://x.com/AlfredoABrown/status/2062272984346231228?s=20). His 28 total [college receptions](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2024/pre-nfl-draft-rookie-rb-dynasty-rankings#/) are a small sample, but his Texas production [rivals Bijan’s](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/1759245639098208561?s=20). Also unlike Hubbard, who went without a *single* explosive run in 2025, Brooks is a [home-run hitter](https://www.cbssports.com/fantasy/football/news/panthers-draft-jonathon-brooks-nfl-profile-fantasy-football-dynasty-outlook-full-scouting-report-more/). Hubbard’s 134 rushes were the most attempts in the *Fantasy Points Data* era [without a single explosive run](https://x.com/KyleM_FF/status/2011212830830444671?s=20).

Over the last three seasons, Hubbard ranks in the bottom 5 of 48 RBs in YPT and YPRR, and, as a runner, below average in YPC, YACO/A, and MTF/A, per *Fantasy Points Data*. His historic lows for explosiveness in 2025 followed historic lows for efficiency in 2024, when he posted the [single worst YPT](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/1947344232039022961?s=20) mark of any player since targets first became a statistic in 1992.

Brooks is unlikely to lead the backfield in Week 1, but his bull case is about how he ends the season, not how he starts. The key to Brooks taking the RB1 reins in 2026 will be how quickly and fully he recovers. He’s on track so far to be at [peak form](https://x.com/mike_e_kaye/status/2063668752428806480?s=20) during the fantasy playoffs.

*Fantasy Points* injury expert Jeff Mueller notes that the timeline and technique used for his surgery are both [good news for Brooks](https://x.com/jmthrivept/status/2055743129408704806?s=20). He is now in month 21 of a process in which performance picks up quite a bit after 16-20 months, and is using a technique with a high rate of durable recovery. Early reports have been [positive](https://www.wsoctv.com/news/local/panthers-running-back-jonathon-brooks-talks-recovery-getting-back-gridiron/7G4HEKPRVZDCZH4QIG7UGE6ORA/) on Brooks coming back strong in 2026.

The strongest sign of his recovery is Carolina’s willingness to [part with](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2062152472127271107?s=20) [Rico Dowdle](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2062152472127271107?s=20). There is every reason to believe Brooks can get close to 100% by the end of this season, and even hitting 90% may be enough for Brooks to [seize this RB1 role](https://x.com/CoachspeakIndex/status/2016685601639326103?s=20).

##### The case for Hubbard

Carolina’s team captain leads early projections by a mile, and the Panthers won’t rush Brooks into seizing the reins in 2026. Unlike Brooks, Hubbard's case relies on proven NFL production rather than projection alone. Hubbard finished RB13 in 2024 with 16.3 FP/G with proven efficiency. He was 12th in YPC (4.78) among backs with 50+ carries and one of only four RBs to finish Top 15 in rushing success rate against both man/gap and zone schemes per *Fantasy Points* *Data*.

Hubbard’s 2025 with zero explosives was an outlier driven by injury. He produced an explosive run rate of 6.0% in 2024 per *Fantasy Points Data*, and his other finishes (3.8% and 4.2%) were respectable. The arrow is [pointing up](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2059644684541063267?s=20) for his future explosive potential after returning to good health. Hubbard missed two games due to a Week 4 calf injury and was never the same after returning. He averaged 14.0 FP/G and 54.3 rushing YPG with a 56.6% success rate after Week 4 but only mustered 6.4 FP/G and 26.7 YPG on a 46.9% success rate after his Week 7 return.

*Fantasy Points’* [projections](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/projections/season/rb) say this race isn’t close. Brooks clocks in at RB39 with 7.95 FP/G and 119.2 total points, light years behind the 192.4 fantasy points and 12.83 FP/G that get Hubbard to RB27. Despite projecting Hubbard for a 21% decrease in average FP/G vs. his 2024 mark, the industry’s sharpest projections still have Hubbard outscoring Brooks by nearly 5 FP/G.

Hubbard is likely to open as the [clear workhorse RB1](https://www.charlotteobserver.com/sports/nfl/carolina-panthers/article315949969.html) per Panthers beat reporter Mike Kaye. This aligns with the *Fantasy Points* projections, which have Hubbard going for nearly 90 more carries and 20 more targets than Brooks over the season.

The excitement for Brooks is through the roof, but Sean Mitchell [wisely asks](https://x.com/smitchell17/status/2063704682174792172?s=20) why the Panthers would race Brooks back or ramp up his touches when they’re paying Hubbard as much as they are. Why risk a prospect with the potential of Brooks after fully guaranteeing Hubbard’s 2026 salary?

It’s easy to wish away inconvenient older RBs, but Ray and JRich from *Wake Up* argue persuasively that Brooks/Hubbard is 2026’s version of the 2025 [Trey/Rhamondre](https://www.youtube.com/live/aoHIlMcn6_o) debate. Rhamondre and Chuba each got paid, [stayed productive](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/1995592635692552675?s=20), and are higher bars for Trey or Brooks to clear than fantasy analysts often credit. [Call the ambulance, but not for Chuba!](https://en.meming.world/wiki/File:Call_An_Ambulance_But_Not_For_Me.jpg/)

##### The judge’s decision

__Hubbard will start and finish the season as Carolina’s RB1.__ __Bet on Brooks in 2027 and beyond, but Chuba will hold him off__ __in 2026.__

Brooks will slowly narrow the gap with Chuba as the season goes along and could produce a handful of spike finishes, but Chuba has a *big* lead in the sharpest projections and is the [better bet](https://x.com/SideHustleFF/status/2078558554114461924?s=20) for season-long formats at equal cost.

The smart strategy for Carolina in 2026 with a high-risk, high-reward asset like Brooks is to ease him in slowly and ride out Hubbard’s [guaranteed money](https://www.nfl.com/news/panthers-rb-chuba-hubbard-agrees-to-four-year-33-2m-contract-extension#:~:text=Hubbard%20has%20agreed%20to%20terms%20on%20a,665%20rushing%20yards%20and%20five%20rushing%20scores.). This front office and coaching staff believe in Brooks, but they signed Chuba to his current extension while Brooks was still healthy in 2024 and have even less incentive to race Brooks back or ramp him up quickly in 2026.

As *Fantasy Points* CEO Scott Barrett notes, Brooks has topped 30 carries in only one of five seasons since leaving high school. Hubbard enters 2026 with strong incumbency advantages and proven top-15 NFL production, whereas Brooks requires a high degree of projection. Even if Brooks hits his ceiling and plays well enough to create a 1A/1B split, it is hard to imagine Carolina throwing caution to the wind and making him a true workhorse RB1. Brooks could be the 1B by the fantasy playoffs, but betting on a speculative, projection-based upside case for Brooks is a lower-ROI outcome than betting on Hubbard’s proven ceiling if he stays healthy.

If Brooks returns to going a full round or more after Hubbard, I’d prefer to buy the upside on Brooks. At their current ADP with a nearly identical price, I’m a strong lean to Hubbard. It’s no fun to draft Chuba, but sometimes you have to eat your vegetables. Derrick Henry once waited behind DeMarco Murray, and TreVeyon Henderson was largely parked behind Rhamondre Stevenson. Brooks is the better bet in 2027 and dynasty, but Chuba is the Carolina RB to draft for 2026.

### __Chicago’s Top Threat:__ Burden, Loveland, or Odunze?

It’s easy to love the 2026 Chicago offense, but it’s harder to figure out who to love most. Which pass catcher wins the Battle of the Bears and leads Chicago in PPR scoring in 2026: Luther Burden, Colston Loveland, or Rome Odunze?

##### The case for and against Burden

Burden is the wild card bet. His elite efficiency and a potential expanded role give him the highest upside of this group, but he also has the widest range of outcomes.

Burden’s rookie year was wickedly efficient. His 2.69 YPRR was the second-best rookie mark of the [past 15 years](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/2038756406711779748?s=20) and the [fourth-highest](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/2057487310321602822?s=20) of any pass catcher, rookie or vet, in 2025. He also finished first among all WRs by a good margin in yards per target over expectation (3.4) per *Fantasy Points Data*, second in YAC/reception (7.23), and fourth in catch rate (78.2%). Burden still has room to grow. He stands to inherit a wealth of vacated targets after producing a [95th percentile](https://www.pff.com/news/fantasy-football-dynasty-values-that-could-skyrocket-in-2026) mark in fantasy points over expectation with a route tree that bears a strong resemblance to [ARSB’s](https://www.si.com/nfl/bears/onsi/luther-burden-vs-rome-odunze-bears-wr1-depth-chart-2026). He earned more crossers and [designed looks](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/49295229/2026-nfl-season-breakout-candidates-burden-bullock-mclaurin) as Ben Johnson’s trust in him grew, and Johnson just warned us all to [buy stock](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/fantasy-factors-nfl-ota-takeaways) in Burden.

That upside is tantalizing, but the risk is real. Burden had only two targets and zero TDs on 28 red-zone routes, and his amazing YPRR number is a potentially misleading [small sample](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/2054937528373829991?s=20). Burden’s 27.8-point explosion in the shootout against the 49ers was his only 20+ point outing, and he produced only a 6/66/0 combined line across two playoff games. Burden was excellent per route, but he was [less efficient in FP/RR and TPRR](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/finding-the-next-jaxon-smith-njigba-playcaller-tendencies#/) than Loveland was, and in a smaller role. The upside is obvious, but so is the extreme variance.

##### The case for and against Loveland

Loveland is the favorite. He has the most certain role and is the most likely to lead Chicago pass catchers in PPR scoring, but comes with a much higher draft cost that may be tough to justify.

Loveland slowly began to take over the Chicago offense midseason, finishing as the TE2 from Weeks 9-18 in total fantasy points. He was first among TEs during that stretch in YPR (12.70) and aDOT (9.30) per *Fantasy Points Data*, and a close second in YPRR (2.37). Things truly took off after Week 15, when Heath notes the Bears shifted half of their offensive snaps to [heavy personnel](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/finding-the-next-jaxon-smith-njigba-playcaller-tendencies#/). Loveland feasted in those sets, recording a 97.8% route participation rate to go with 4.66 YPRR. The final four games saw him log an average of 11.8 targets and 19.9 fantasy points per game, [pacing Chicago](https://www.espn.com/fantasy/football/story/_/id/48940783/2026-fantasy-football-rankings-draft-value-risk) in targets.

Johnson did hype up Burden, but the [former TE coach](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/49267903/ranking-nfl-top-10-tight-ends-2026-execs-coaches-scouts) also promised to open up the [route tree](https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/bears-te-colston-loveland-predicted-130024549.html) for his young breakout TE. Beyond simply being the [top option](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/49267903/ranking-nfl-top-10-tight-ends-2026-execs-coaches-scouts) in Chicago, Loveland could more than justify his price tag by climbing past [Brock Bowers](https://www.4for4.com/2026/preseason/2026-fantasy-football-rankings-breakdown-tight-ends) or [Trey McBride](https://www.fantasypros.com/2026/07/dynasty-fantasy-football-rankings-advice-tight-ends-2026/). Loveland’s outstanding efficiency across a range of metrics from Weeks 9-18 means he only needs to maintain his current role to vault to a TE1 finish.

The hype train for Loveland has driven up his price, and Fantasy Points CEO Scott Barrett cautions that we should perhaps [pump the brakes](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/2072720159341494337?s=20) on Loveland at cost. Drafting Loveland requires paying a [king’s ransom at TE](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/brain-trust-favorite-sleeper-tight-end#/) when you could get [comparable production](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/2072751408152293705?s=20) from other TEs later in drafts. You could draft Tee Higgins, who averaged 17.5 FP/G with Joe Burrow the past two years, at the same price. You could get Odunze two rounds later.

Loveland’s Round 4 draft cost requires you to draft him at his ceiling on the basis of a [very small sample](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/2072726301895442560?s=20). Taking a TE before Round 6 is a lot like coming at the king: if you’re going to take a swing, [you best not miss](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/2072764094885539855?s=20). Loveland had a great finish, but can he do it with a [healthy Odunze and a full-time Burden](https://www.fantasypros.com/nfl/players/colston-loveland.php)? It’s not always roses for Ben Johnson’s TEs, even after a [great rookie season](https://www.profootballnetwork.com/fantasy-football/sam-laporta-fantasy-projection-2025/).

##### The case for and against Odunze

Odunze is the injury discount bet and goes two rounds later, but he has WR1 upside. He charged out of the gates with 19.9 FP/G as the fantasy WR3 from Weeks 1-4 and now stands to inherit many vacated targets, but he also carries big downside risk due to injury and variance.

Odunze ranks 9th in [end zone targets](https://www.espn.com/fantasy/football/story/_/id/48940783/2026-fantasy-football-rankings-draft-value-risk) since being drafted in 2024, and the early-season display of talent in 2025 [was real](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2076887541672812919?s=20). It was a tale of two seasons, as *Fantasy Points* contributor Kyle Menton notes his 0.452 [average separation score](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2025/statistically-significant-average-separation-score#/) (ASS) over the first four weeks collapsed to 0.038 post-injury to end the season. There’s a clear case for positive regression entering 2026, where Menton likes Odunze over Burden as the [bigger beneficiary](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/2025-ceiling-adjusted-fpg-wide-receivers) of DJ Moore and Olamide Zaccheaus’ vacated targets.

Aside from holding off Burden and Loveland, the big question is how well Odunze can return from injury. Early reports are mixed. *Fantasy Points* Injury Expert Jeff Mueller calls for caution, noting that Odunze is in a 1-2 year “remodeling” phase with a [5-7x recurrence risk](https://x.com/jmthrivept/status/2063283981127418305?s=20) due to altered biomechanics and compensatory injury risks that could require a future surgery. Odunze raised further alarm bells by calling this his “[new normal](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/fantasy-factors-nfl-ota-takeaways),” and Mueller warned fantasy managers that there is [zero way around](https://x.com/jmthrivept/status/2077948639360741557?s=20) the heightened risk.

Add in scoring only 7.6 FP/G with a 38.2% catch rate from Weeks 9-18 per *Fantasy Points Data*, the sixth-most [drops](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/2025-ceiling-adjusted-fpg-wide-receivers#/) (including one on a potential [playoff TD](https://www.si.com/nfl/bears/onsi/luther-burden-vs-rome-odunze-bears-wr1-depth-chart-2026)), and 37.7% of his fantasy points being [TD-driven](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/2025-ceiling-adjusted-fpg-wide-receivers#/), and it may be wiser to pay up for Loveland or to take the upside bet on Burden.

##### The judge’s decision

__Loveland will be Chicago’s PPR leader__ __and earn the lion’s share of looks in a dangerous passing offense. His strong floor and TE1 ceiling justify the cost.__

The *Fantasy Points* projections have Loveland at 12.4 FP/G, only narrowly ahead of Odunze (12.1) and Burden (11.6). That may look like a coin flip and feels like a potential overpay to some sharp drafters in Round 4.

But Loveland goes as early as the [2.03](https://x.com/TheOGfantasy/status/2077893436208787595?s=20) in other high-stakes dynasty startups, and his Round 4 price will be remembered as a heist if Loveland finishes TE1. There’s a plausible path to Loveland as both the clear top option in Chicago and the TE1 following his finish to 2025.

The upside case for each Bear is reasonable, but the downside risks to Odunze and Burden are realistic and highly plausible. Every potential setback for Odunze or Burden would expand Loveland’s role inside fantasy’s most explosive offense.

Loveland is worth the Round 4 cost. I prefer other options late Round 3, and I don’t feel awful about Burden in late Round 4 or Odunze at any point in Round 6 or beyond. At their current ADP, Loveland has both the best floor and ceiling case to produce strong ROI at cost.

### Conclusion

Every year, championships are won or lost based on the outcomes of a few critical debates. Making firm calls on the toughest decisions is a humbling task, but following the evidence and weighing each case with an open mind produces a lasting edge and more sound decisions.

Our final decisions are:

+ De’Von Achane can be a Top 5 RB in just about any offense.
+ Chuba Hubbard will lead Carolina in 2026. Brooks will overtake him in 2027.
+ Loveland is the best of the Bears’ pass catchers, and he is worth his Round 4 cost.

For a *good value pick*, think of it as “if I draft this guy at pick (x) or later, I’m getting solid value.” For a *bad value pick*, it lists the point when a pick is a reach. full_text:
Mid-July typically means hanging out at the pool, taking a trip to the beach, or grilling out in the backyard. However, for some NFL teams, work is about to start, as rookie report dates are quickly approaching. All teams will be fully reported to training by July 28, but some will have their rookies report over the next few days.

It’s an exciting time on the football calendar, as everyone gets back together and is looking forward to a (hopefully) successful campaign. However, success looks different across the league. Certain players could be on the verge of career-bests, but stuck on a 3-14 team. Hello, __Trey McBride__, who saw career-highs in targets (169), receptions (126), yards (1,239), and touchdowns (11).

So, who is this year’s Trey McBride? I’m going to take a look at six guys I feel are poised for a breakout season in 2026. They don’t have to become first-team All-Pros like McBride. The two quarterbacks certainly won’t be, but I think each of these guys is in line for a big season, given their abilities, coaching staffs, and positional situations.

Again, these breakdowns are based on what I saw from these players on film last year, the trajectory of their careers so far, and the opportunities I think they’ll have given the rest of the roster. Let’s get into it.

### __Malik Willis__ (QB, MIA)

Willis finally gets a chance to be a full-time starter after signing with Miami this offseason. The 2022 third-round pick has had a tough road to this point, appearing in 22 games with just six starts. He was never “the guy” in Tennessee, then he sat behind __Jordan Love__ for most of his tenure in Green Bay. That said, he made the most of his opportunity in 2025 and parlayed that into his new three-year contract.

Willis was one of the more “upside”-oriented quarterback prospects coming out of school in 2022. My fellow scouts with the Brows recognized the raw talent (arm strength, speed, athleticism), but we all questioned what it would look like in an NFL system. He got off to a very rough start, but by the end of 2025, Willis looked like a poised facilitator for the Packers.

For Miami to have success, Willis will have to attempt many more than the 70 passes he threw over his two years in Green Bay. I don’t think he’ll lead the league in passing or even sniff the top 10, but a simplified attack that utilizes his athletic ability should open the door for Willis to have a solid season. Enter __Bobby Slowik__.

Slowik survived __Jeff Hafley__’s hiring and enters his first year as Miami’s offensive coordinator. Things didn’t end well in Houston for Slowik, but remember that he was the mastermind behind __C.J. Stroud__’s 2023 OROY season. Houston had enough of a run game to complement Stroud’s arm, and I think Miami has to have a similar philosophy: play action, rollouts, QB-run game.

__De’Von Achane__ and __Ollie Gordon__ could become one of the better rushing duos in the league, so Willis should rely on these two to take some pressure off of him. I’m not expecting an overly explosive passing attack with this receiver group, and I’m not super high on the Dolphins’ [offensive line](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/season/2026/nfl-offensive-line-rankings#/) (22nd), but Willis can finally play free and show everyone what he’s got.

### __Tyler Shough__ (QB, NO)

I was not that excited about __Tyler Shough__ heading into 2025. Coming out, I thought he had a bunch of good/above-average traits, but nothing that really got me jazzed up. The fact that he couldn’t beat out __Spencer Rattler__ to start the season made me think I was right. However, Shough’s second half of 2025 proved me wrong.

After taking over as the starter in Week 9, Shough totaled 2,384 yards, 10 touchdowns, and six interceptions. He also completed 67.6% of his passes, which is impressive for a rookie. Shough threw for 250+ yards each of the final four weeks and was a relatively clean operator as the Saints somehow crept back into the NFC South race.

You can argue that Shough played some meaningless games, but he likely has the most momentum of any Year 2 quarterback.

I’m high on Shough because of his play-calling and supporting cast. Is he ready to be a “win because of” guy? Probably not yet. But __Chris Olave__ can make any quarterback look good, the Saints added __Jordyn Tyson__, the running back room is dangerous, and the offensive line is improved. Year two of __Kellen Moore__ should be a noticeable step forward, as the play-calling head coach gets more comfortable with his QB.

Shough has a better chance of sneaking into the top-10 in passing than Willis, and should be a reliable later-round QB option.

### __R.J. Harvey__ (RB, DEN)

Denver has a crowded running back room with __J.K. Dobbins__, __Jaleel McLaughlin__, and __Tyler Badie__ returning, and fourth-round pick __Jonah Coleman__ entering the fold. So how is __R.J. Harvey__ supposed to break out? I firmly believe that __Sean Payton__ wants Harvey to become “the guy” in Denver’s backfield, and he’ll get him the ball in multiple ways.

Dobbins was the lead ball carrier until suffering a Week 10 Lisfranc injury. Harvey became the starter, but wasn’t overly impactful on the ground. However, he was a reliable receiving option all season. Harvey was fourth on the team with 47 receptions and proved to Payton that he can be productive in this phase.

On the ground, Harvey had his most success with downhill/gap runs. I expect Payton to favor that when Harvey is in the game, especially since he’ll be running behind the best offensive line in the game. Payton wants to be the smartest guy in the room, so don’t be surprised if there’s a balanced touch count between Dobbins, Harvey, and someone else. That said, I still believe Harvey is the lead ball-carrier of choice.

Before the Dobbins injury, Harvey saw more than seven carries just once through the first 10 weeks. He then saw fewer than 11 only once down the stretch. I mentioned the crowded Denver backfield, but Payton made it clear he really only wanted to use Dobbins and Harvey when everyone was healthy last season. As long as Harvey stays out of the doghouse, he should see a healthy dose of carries and targets.

### __TreVeyon Henderson__ (RB, NE)

It’s tough to say that Henderson didn’t already break out in year one. He led the Patriots in rushing (911) and scrimmage yards (1,132), and was a big play waiting to happen. The natural quickness and long speed he has are uncanny, and Henderson was a perfect complement to __Rhamondre Stevenson__.

Henderson and Stevenson are an excellent “thunder and lightning” combination, but I think the second-year RB is ready to take the reins. Stevenson has one more year of guaranteed money, so it likely won’t be Henderson’s backfield this year. But the Ohio State product proved he can carry the load when Stevenson missed three games midseason.

I see this situation similar to when we drafted __Nick Chubb__ in Cleveland. __Carlos Hyde__ had been signed that offseason as the veteran ball-carrier, and everyone expected Chubb to need some time to develop. Hyde only lasted six games before we traded him, and Chubb never gave up the starting job.

Stevenson, obviously, remained the starter when healthy, but Henderson should be the lead back in my opinion. He’s incredibly explosive on the ground and can be deadly out of the backfield. I’d entertain an argument about not wanting to overwork him early in his career, but Henderson can be a bellcow. He’s the man in 2026.

### __Emeka Egbuka__ (WR, TB)

__Mike Evans__ leaving Tampa Bay throws the door wide open for __Emeka Egbuka__ to become the Buccaneers’ No. 1 option. Egbuka paid immediate dividends after Evans’ Week 3 hamstring injury sidelined him for three games. The rookie posted 101 and 163 yards in back-to-back weeks, proving that he can be the main option in Tampa Bay’s passing attack.

He managed more than 64 yards just once after that, but I’d put that on an injury-plagued __Baker Mayfield__ being under duress behind a banged-up offensive line more than Egbuka hitting the rookie wall. Egbuka finished 10th in the league with 127 targets as a rookie and had an aDOT of 12.9. That number was second on the team for receivers with 10+ targets (Evans led that category at 14.1). Mayfield got comfortable with Egbuka quickly last year and should continue to feed him the ball.

Looking at the rest of Tampa’s receiving options, __Jalen McMillan__ and __Chris Godwin__ are the next two options. I’ve always really liked Godwin, but he’s getting older, and I’m not convinced he’s 100% back from the 2024 ankle injury. McMillan is a solid No. 2 who can be elevated by a productive option on the other side. He’s also coming back from a season-ending neck injury. __Cade Otton__ ended 2025 second on the team with 80 targets, so expect him to be Mayfield’s security blanket once again.

All this tells me is that Egbuka is set up to be WR1 for the Bucs. He essentially was last year when Evans went down, but there’s no questioning it now, in my opinion. I think he easily tops 1,000 yards and 100 catches in year two.
